tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (benchmarks/filter_comparison.cu, which includes cuco/bloom_filter.cuh and runs GBBF side by side under Google Benchmark). Flags are in meson.build (optimization=3, C++20, nvcc --expt-extended-lambda/--expt-relaxed-constexpr with sm_80/90/120 gencode). The arXiv paper's setup names CUDA 13.2 and the full hardware: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell on an AMD EPYC 7713P host, plus a Xeon W9-3595X for the CPU baseline.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per the README tables (Config<31,28,16,4>, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell): vs GPU Blocked Bloom Filter (cuCollections GBBF), 9.1x faster insert and 7.7x faster query on the ~100M k-mer C. elegans filter, and 8.2x insert and 7.6x query on the ~3.1B k-mer CHM13 filter. Other baselines: CPU Super Bloom 59-234x (92x/234x small, 59x/165x large); Cuckoo-GPU 7.8-3427x (80x/8.0x small, 3427x/7.8x large); Bulk TCF 12-67x; GQF 11-69x (69x/13x small, 42x/11x large).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CUDA 13.2 (nvcc, per the paper's experimental setup); meson.build default_options optimization=3 (-O3), cpp_std=c++20, warning_level=2; nvcc args -std=c++20 --expt-extended-lambda --expt-relaxed-constexpr --generate-line-info -gencode sm_80/sm_90/sm_120. GCC/Clang host compiler, version not stated. Meson/Ninja build, Google Benchmark.
corrections.hardware: GPU runs: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB GDDR7) on an AMD EPYC 7713P (64-core) host, AlmaLinux 10.1 (paper System A); the paper also reports GH200 (System B). CPU Super Bloom baseline: Intel Xeon W9-3595X (60 cores, 120 threads, 256 GB DDR5).
corrections.caveats: Very new project (7 stars). The paper (arXiv:2606.24417, June 2026) is a preprint and not yet peer-reviewed. All benchmark numbers are first-party and not independently reproduced, though the benchmark code, build flags, CUDA version and hardware are all public. One comparison baseline, Cuckoo-GPU (tdortman/Cuckoo-GPU), is by the same author and already in the known list, so this entry's primary claim is the result against the cuCollections GBBF Bloom filter. The 3427x Cuckoo-GPU insert figure is a large-filter outlier; most other ratios are in the single or double digits.

notes: The README numbers match the record except two ranges: Cuckoo-GPU spans 7.8-3427x (not 8.0-3427x) and GQF spans 11-69x (not 13-69x). The CPU Super Bloom runs used an Intel Xeon, but the host CPU for the GPU runs was an AMD EPYC 7713P. I kept tier A because the code, flags, compiler (CUDA 13.2) and hardware are all public or stated.

tier_reason: The README has first-party go test numbers from public benchmark code (qf_test.go BenchmarkBloomFilter / BenchmarkUnpackedFilterLookup / BenchmarkPackedFilterLookup, against bits-and-blooms/bloom/v3 v3.0.1) on an Apple M1. The Go toolchain version is never stated (go.mod only declares go 1.20), so methodology is partial. That matches the earlier ribbongo precedent, which was tiered C for unstated Go version.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Lookup: unpacked quotient filter 20.43 ns/op and packed 30.95 ns/op vs bits-and-blooms/bloom v3 Bloom filter 74.47 ns/op, about 3.6x and 2.4x faster (derived from page data). The README text itself says "about 4 times faster". A native Go map lookup is shown for reference at 9.373 ns/op.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain, version not stated (go.mod declares go 1.20); `go test -run=xxx -bench=.` with default build flags
corrections.caveats: Single first-party go test run on one laptop (Apple M1), with no repeated trials or variance and no Go version stated; the README numbers date from an August 2021 README update. The benchmark only does positive lookups, cycling through keys that were all inserted. The Bloom filter is built with bloom.NewWithEstimates(n, 0.0001). The baseline is one third-party Go library (bits-and-blooms/bloom v3.0.1), not a canonical C/C++ implementation. The README's own "about 4 times faster" wording overstates the measured 3.6x.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly. I downgraded A to C because the compiler (Go version) is unstated and ribbongo was tiered C on the same grounds. Metadata checks out: MIT, 96 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-09-25, which is just over 12 months before today, so stale.

tier_reason: The claims come from a peer-reviewed SIGMOD 2017 paper (DOI 10.1145/3035918.3035963, pp. 775-787, confirmed via Crossref) that benchmarks against Bloom and counting Bloom filters. The morning paper page quotes them verbatim. It is not A: the repo's own src/bm.c benchmarks only the CQF (through gqf_wrapper.h) with no Bloom baseline, and I could not open the paper to check its compiler and CPU details.

corrections.caveats: The claims are qualitative (up to an order of magnitude, several times, at least 2x) with no exact figures. They are the paper authors' own statements, quoted verbatim on blog.acolyer.org ("the morning paper"), not independent measurements by the blog. I could not fetch the paper PDF: dl.acm.org and the author's Stony Brook PDF both returned 403, although Semantic Scholar lists the paper as gold open access. The repo's bm.c benchmarks only the CQF and has no Bloom baseline code. The Makefile builds with gcc -Ofast -msse4.2 and needs Haswell+ for the fast select path (NH=1 for older CPUs).

notes: The quotes match the blog page verbatim, and the page does compare against Bloom and counting Bloom filters. Metadata checks out: BSD-3-Clause, 132 stars, not archived, last commit 2022-09-22, so abandoned. I could not verify the claim about genomics tools using it and left it uncorrected.
